title: Optimal low-rank compression of quantum dynamics
authors: Hugo Mackay, Donghoon Kim, Tan Van Vu, Tomotaka Kuwahara
abstract: Local quantum interactions generate dynamics in an exponentially large Hilbert space, yet locality and entanglement restrict the information that can spread and accumulate. Bounds on propagation and entanglement growth, together with tensor networks, exploit these restrictions to discard information unnecessary for describing the evolution. This leads to a sharper question: how much information must any low-rank representation retain? Here we determine these limits, up to logarithmic factors, for short-range interactions. For time-independent evolution, the optimal rank obeys $\log D=\widetilde O(t+\sqrt{\log(1/ε)})$, with matching lower bounds fixing the accuracy exponent $1/2$; for arbitrary driving, matching fixed-time bounds instead give $2/3$. Correspondingly, the corresponding dynamical entanglement spectra exhibit distinct small-$α$ Rényi laws, $α^{-1}$ and $α^{-2}$. In one dimension, the static limit is constructively attained by an explicit MPO algorithm, with an analogous extension to Liouvillian dynamics. Together, these results determine the irreducible information required to represent local quantum evolution and uncover distinct entanglement structures in static and driven dynamics.
summary: This paper establishes rigorous bounds on the minimum information content required to simulate local quantum dynamics. By comparing static versus time-dependent driving, the authors show that the required computational complexity differs significantly. These results provide a deep understanding of the fundamental entanglement structures governing quantum evolution.
main_problem: The paper determines the minimum information (low-rank complexity) required to accurately represent the time evolution generated by local quantum interactions in an exponentially large Hilbert space.
main_result: The optimal compression law differs significantly between static (time-independent) and arbitrarily driven quantum dynamics, with the static case requiring less information than the driven case.
method: The authors utilize tensor networks, specifically analyzing the Buffered Schmidt Rank (BSR), to quantify the required low-rank representation needed to bound the error in approximating the time evolution operator.
model_or_system: The study considers quantum many-body systems on a lattice ($\Lambda$) governed by local Markovian dynamics, described by either a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(	au)$ or a Lindblad master equation $L(	au)$.
key_observables: Low-rank complexity ($D_\epsilon$), dynamical entanglement spectra, and the Buffered Schmidt Rank (BSR).
important_parameters: Time ($t$), accuracy ($\epsilon$), and the nature of the driving (static vs. arbitrary).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption of exponentially decaying local interactions and the use of tensor network techniques to exploit locality bounds.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the extremal compression laws for static versus driven evolution and illustrates the distinct small-alpha Rényi scaling ($\alpha^{-1}$ vs. $\alpha^{-2}$) for the entanglement spectra.
paper_structure: The paper develops the problem by first establishing the general framework using tensor networks and locality bounds. It then derives specific scaling laws for static and driven dynamics, culminating in constructive algorithms for the 1D case and detailed analysis of entanglement spectra.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental, quantitative bounds on the complexity of quantum information storage and processing, directly impacting how we model and simulate complex, interacting quantum systems in condensed matter theory.
